title: [B2 • Band 6.0] Bài 220: The Demise of the Mental Map
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 220 (LEVEL B2 • BAND 6.0)

The Demise of the Mental Map: Spatial Cognition in the Digital Age

Paragraph A. For tens of thousands of years, navigating physical terrain was an indispensable human survival skill. Whether tracking herds across open plains or crossing uncharted oceans by the stars, our ancestors relied on internal spatial mapping. Inside the human brain, dedicated neural circuits constantly calculate positions, monitor direction, and construct three-dimensional mental models of our surroundings. Over the last two decades, however, the near-universal adoption of satellite GPS smartphone apps has disrupted this evolutionary partnership. Rather than actively surveying streets and connecting visual cues into mental maps, modern travellers passively obey turn-by-turn voice instructions.

Paragraph B. The biological command hub for spatial navigation lies inside the hippocampus, a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the brain's medial temporal lobe. In the early 2000s, British neuroscientist Dr. Eleanor Maguire studied licensed London taxi drivers, who must spend three to four years memorising 'The Knowledge'—twenty-five thousand streets and thousands of landmarks within six miles of Charing Cross. Maguire found that qualified cabbies had a significantly larger posterior hippocampus than ordinary citizens, and grey matter volume grew steadily with years on the job, proving active navigation physically enlarges neural structures.

Paragraph C. Under automated GPS guidance, however, this neural network falls silent. Neuroimaging experiments show that when volunteers travel through a city using passive device prompts, activation in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex flatlines. Unlike active route-finding, which demands spatial calculation and decision-making at every junction, following arrows requires only minimal reaction. Navigators develop 'tunnel vision', overlooking peripheral features and failing to build a coherent overview of city layouts. Consequently, if a signal drops or a battery dies, users frequently become lost even along daily routes.

Paragraph D. The long-term medical implications of losing spatial exercise are raising concern among geriatric neurologists. Epidemiological data confirm that the hippocampus is among the earliest regions harmed by Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia, with spatial disorientation frequently appearing as the first clinical symptom. Because cognitive reserve—the brain's defence against age-related decline—is built through lifelong mental exertion, scientists warn that chronic dependence on digital directions may deprive the hippocampus of vital stimulation.

Paragraph E. To reverse this trend, cognitive psychologists advocate practising 'spatial hygiene'. Researchers encourage people to deliberately switch off GPS guidance along familiar local journeys, compelling the brain to observe environmental cues, link intersections mentally, and judge distances on its own. Treating everyday commutes as gentle mental workouts helps maintain active neural pathways well into old age.

Paragraph F. At the same time, software designers are developing 'cognitively supportive' navigation tools. Rather than issuing blind turn-by-turn commands, experimental apps offer spoken cues anchored to prominent local features—such as 'turn right after the stone cathedral'—or display zoomed-out overview maps that keep users oriented within the wider landscape. Protecting our natural ability to navigate is not merely about convenience; it is about safeguarding the physical resilience of the human brain.

q1.text: medical evidence linking poor navigation skills to early symptoms of brain illness

steps: Đoạn D: Mất định hướng không gian là triệu chứng lâm sàng sớm của Alzheimer và sa sút trí tuệ mạch máu.

q2.text: proof that years of active route memorisation physically enlarge a brain region

steps: Đoạn B: Nghiên cứu của Eleanor Maguire trên tài xế taxi London.

q3.text: examples of redesigned digital apps that encourage active environmental awareness

steps: Đoạn F: Ứng dụng thế hệ mới chỉ đường bằng công trình nổi bật hoặc bản đồ thu phóng bao quát.

q4.text: brain-scan findings showing how passive arrows silence navigation circuits

steps: Đoạn C: Chụp não cho thấy hoạt động vùng hồi hải mã tắt lịm (flatlines) khi đi theo GPS thụ động.

q5.text: London cabbies who fail 'The Knowledge' exam are allowed to retake it after six months.

steps: Đoạn B: Bài nhắc tới việc học 'The Knowledge' mất 3–4 năm, không hề đề cập quy định thi lại.

q6.text: Following automated turn-by-turn prompts makes travellers ignore features around them.

steps: Đoạn C: Người dùng bị 'tunnel vision', bỏ qua các đặc điểm xung quanh (overlooking peripheral features).

q7.text: Relying on GPS every day strengthens the hippocampus against age-related decline.

steps: Đoạn D: Phụ thuộc GPS làm não thiếu kích thích nhận thức cần thiết, không thể giúp tăng sức đề kháng não.

q8.text: Protecting natural navigation skills helps safeguard the physical health of the brain.

steps: Đoạn F: "...safeguarding the physical resilience of the human brain."
Đoạn B: "...command hub for spatial navigation lies inside the hippocampus..."
Đoạn B: "...twenty-five thousand streets and thousands of landmarks..."
Đoạn F: "...turn right after the stone cathedral..."
